To merge results from ab initio method streams for heavy nuclei, stream outputs are combined early in the calculation process, specifically during the construction of the nuclear matrix elements. This is done by merging the streams after the generation of the nuclear wave functions and nuclear-energy spectra. A new procedure, called the Merging Stream approach, has been developed to combine the streams at this early stage, thereby reducing the computational overhead associated with re-running the calculation for each new nuclear charge. The Merging Stream approach is based on the concept of removing streams that are irrelevant to the final calculation outcomes and is achieved by introducing a stream selection criterion. This new technique enables the rapid combination of stream outputs for an infinite range of new nuclear charges with minimal additional computational cost. The Merging Stream approach is shown to provide accurate results in 6He, 6Li, 16C, and 17O calculations.

We invite readers to join us on a journey into the world of topological quantum physics, using the celebrated Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model as our guide. This iconic model not only sparked the concept of topological insulators over three decades ago, but also continues to captivate researchers with its intricate concepts and the numerous ways to teach them. From exploring various interpretations and visualizations of topological charges, to delving into the resolutions of popular homework problems assigned to graduate students, our goal is to offer a comprehensive and unified perspective on these concepts. Additionally, we examine the relevance of SSH model in condensed matter physics and the rapid progress it has facilitated in the field. With its enduring significance, SSH model provides an ideal framework to introduce essential ideas in topological quantum physics, making it accessible and understandable to a broad range of audiences.

This study examines the compactness of composition operators within Bergman spaces associated with certain bounded, convex domains in complex n-dimensional space containing non-trivial analytic circles in complex 1-dimensional space. It's established that a composition operator is compact if and only if its symbol, the composition of a bounded analytic function in complex 1-dimensional space with an element of the Bergman space, is bounded or has a bounded norm within the closed unit disk in complex 1-dimensional space. This condition is specifically tight for operators that compose functions with analytic weights. Furthermore, a key criterion for determining compactness has been identified in relation to the gradient of the weighted hyperbolic metric within the ambient convex domain. To complement these findings, a counterexample has been constructed to demonstrate that the established sufficient condition for compactness is not necessarily a necessary condition.

We derived the two-loop amplitude for five-dimensional supergravity in the AdS$_5$ space using an approach that translates QFT principles directly, specifically by converting QFT correlations into supergravity amplitudes via a proven theorem. In doing so, we successfully computed the two-loop supergravity amplitude, which we then verified matches the previously established two-loop Weyl anomaly in four-dimensional conformal field theory when reduced to the AdS$_5$ boundary conditions.

This paper introduces DynaSOAr, a parallel memory allocator designed for use on GPUs with multiple threads per block. It is specifically tailored for use in object-based programming on these devices, addressing the long-standing challenge of memory allocation on GPUs with multiple threads per block. DynaSOAr operates on a per-block basis, utilizing shared memory to manage memory allocation, free memory, and track memory usage without relying on global memory or per-thread stack variables. It achieves this through the implementation of a circular array, providing a means to dynamically allocate and manage memory on a per-block basis. By using a parallel approach to free memory, DynaSOAr is capable of handling highly unbalanced workloads without slowing down memory allocation. In addition, DynaSOAr provides a means to dynamically set the memory alignment, enabling developers to optimize memory usage for small memory allocations. It is highly efficient, with over 90% efficiency in memory usage for large simulations. It outperforms other allocators in both speed and memory usage, demonstrating superior results in benchmark tests and real-world applications.

We propose two standard $U(1)_X$ models, motivated by the $SO(10)$ framework, with unusual gauge symmetry characteristics. The first model has a unique $U(1)_X$ intersection with $SU(2)_L \times SU(3)_C$ as large as $U(1)_{B-L}$ but has a significantly smaller coupling than expected. In addition, this model is distinct from the $U(1)_{B3R}$ model commonly studied in doublet dark matter contexts. On the other hand, the second model has a large $U(1)_X$ intersection with $SU(2)_L \times SU(3)_C$ similar to $U(1)_{B-L}$ yet exhibits LHC dissimilarities. We thoroughly examine the leptoquark phenomenology induced by the $U(1)_X$ interaction in both models, using the diphoton excess as a focal point at the LHC.

Understanding how the properties of materials and constructions of objects respond to strain is crucial. Investigating the mechanical properties of a cane tube, which is a hollow cylinder made of metal and used in biomedical applications such as stent development, through experimental and computational analysis for its strain-stress properties and stability under pressure revealed its ability to withstand strain up to 6% due to its strong material properties and structural integrity. However, this research also showed that the inner surface of the tube experiences significant variations in strain, which may impact its biomedical applications and lead to mechanical instability at specific pressure levels and axial strains within a particular range. Furthermore, the findings of this research can be applied to the design and development of other engineered microstructures used in a wide range of technological and biomedical applications.

In various fields, Bayesian networks have become indispensable tools for modeling, inference, and decision-making, given their ability to capture complex, probabilistically dependent phenomena. While traditional Bayesian networks define probability distributions precisely, their limitations arise from the necessity of well-specified joint distributions, which is often impractical due to limitations on storage and computation. To address these issues, researchers have explored the concept of robust Bayesian networks, where the network structure and parameter uncertainty are tolerated to varying degrees based on specified bounds. Although methods exist for analyzing the consistency of such networks under specified bounds, the lack of efficient tools for quantifying uncertainty within these frameworks hinders their practical use. This study addresses this gap by developing an innovative framework that enables the efficient computation of bounds on key uncertainty metrics, which are then demonstrated to ensure the robustness of our network models. The framework's versatility allows it to accommodate a wide range of uncertainty models, including those founded on measures such as KL divergence and forward divergence, as well as those based on total variation. The research demonstrates that exact calculations for the most complex models are achievable via transformation into probabilistic circuits, marking a significant advancement. The study further presents an alternative approach using simplified variants, which is remarkably efficient, requiring nothing more than polynomial-time computation. The findings are substantiated through the evaluation of concrete robust Bayesian networks.

In this study, we demonstrate Wannier-Thrimer-Bloch oscillations in an acoustic wave context by exploring the behavior of a sonoluminescent system driven by standing waves. To accomplish this, we analyze a sonoluminescent model modified to include two discrete energy levels and a quantum coherence term between these levels and an external acoustic drive. Using two approaches - a semiclassical method and numerical integration, we show that the dynamics of the system can be represented using Wannier-Stanley matrices. These matrices enable us to express acoustic Wannier-Stilb oscillations as well as establish a relationship between Floquet states and Wannier-Stilb states.

In the context of generalised quadrangles, we focus on investigating local transitivity within the automorphism groups of the quadrangles. It is demonstrated that local transitivity on vertices or edges implies a specific spread or partial spread when combined with a particular subset of quadrangles. Furthermore, it is shown that local transitivity on vertices or edges, in conjunction with a particular subset of quadrangles, serves as a necessary and sufficient condition for the quadrangles to form a neighbour-transitive code. Example spreads and quadrangles are provided to illustrate these concepts.

We use recent 2D maps of the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) density variations to establish an anisotropic density model. Our analysis relies on calculating the correlation function of density distributions at multiple scales and orientations. By comparing the results with isotropic and anisotropic models, we determine the most suitable density variation patterns. With further examination, we identify the most plausible carbon star efficiency and atomic hydrogen abundance ranges in the CMZ. Our study provides insight into the complex, direction-dependent density patterns in the CMZ, which is crucial for understanding the region's formation history.

To better comprehend the transient behavior of electron dynamics near a heavily excited atom, a simplified mathematical model is introduced, focusing on electron groups instead of individual electrons. This approach allows for the derivation of a closed-form expression relating electron density to excitation intensity, which is in accordance with experimental findings. By utilizing this relationship, the impact of electron groups on X-ray Absorption Near-Edge Spectra can be effectively accounted for, thereby justifying the utilization of a simplified rate-based model for interpreting Non-linear X-ray Absorption Spectroscopy outcomes.

A microtemperature sensor featuring a unified CMFB architecture has been introduced, which uses a single operational amplifier and has a wide input voltage range covering the subthreshold region. This integrated circuit, fabricated using a 0.5-micron process, has a small footprint of 0.021mm$^2$. Each temperature sensing unit incorporates a fully integrated resistor with a precision of $\pm$5%, which enables the conversion of temperature to resistance. This conversion is then converted to a digital format with 8 bits, utilizing a conventional counter-based counting circuit, resulting in a measurement accuracy of $\pm$1.4 degrees Celsius. Various measurement modes demonstrate the versatility of this design in achieving distinct trade-offs between energy consumption, resolution, and inaccuracy. Furthermore, measurements in a real-world environment have shown that the designed temperature sensor adheres to these specifications with a high level of consistency, remaining accurate even in the presence of significant vibration and motion.

Quantum entanglement serves as the core functionality in numerous quantum technologies. Heralded generation of entangled states is deemed essential for widespread use due to its abundance of entangled pairs, despite presenting technical challenges. Our research focuses on producing polarization-entangled photons utilizing a quantum-scissors-based approach. This method is notable for its versatility and ability to create vast amounts of entangled pairs, as well as its reliance on relatively simple and robust setup configurations. Our results demonstrate the successful production of polarization-entangled photons and quantify the errors associated with this process. These outcomes not only showcase the potential of the quantum-scissors technique for entanglement creation but also highlight its promise for applications where numerous entangled pairs are required.

This research explores the concept of digital metric spaces and spanners within the context of these spaces. By defining a digital metric on the integer grid of a Euclidean space, a digital spanner can be created that approximates the original Euclidean distance with an optimal ratio. Our study focuses on developing digital spanners for general Euclidean spaces without a specific dimension. Our first contribution is the construction of a digital spanner with a logarithmic number of vertices that achieves a O(log n) stretch factor. This is not only an improvement over previous methods but also confirms a conjecture that such a spanner exists. Additionally, our work involves examining lower bound theories, and we discover that a stretch factor of Ω(log n / log log n) is achievable.

Accurate IoT data analysis heavily relies on IoT device profiling, which in turn hinges on effective feature selection. The complexity of IoT environments, which are characterized by massive data streams and resource-constrained devices, presents significant challenges. This difficulty is compounded by the lack of a standardized approach for choosing suitable features. This article contributes to resolving this issue by introducing a novel, cost-aware approach to feature selection, which exploits the uniqueness of IoT environments to minimize costs and improve accuracy. This method utilizes the diversity of IoT environments to determine an optimal feature subset at a lower cost. Furthermore, this approach is enhanced by a feature subset validation mechanism to ensure the reliability and validity of its findings. The article also compares different optimization techniques to facilitate this process, which includes adapting the PSO to the complexities of IoT environments. The proposed approach is verified by experiments using real-world data from 8 IoT domains, which demonstrate its superiority to existing methods.

Godel modal logic's sound and complete set of axioms serves as the basis for an ordered set of logics obtained by adding one additional unary connective at a time.  The first-order semantics system featuring a binary relation and a corresponding modal algebra can be utilized to interpret the extensions of Godel modal logic.  This paper explores the various modal algebras and relational structures associated with these extensions,  focusing on the properties of finite distributive lattices with an order- topological mean (OTM) and a weak positive mean (WPM).  Additionally,  it provides dualities for Godel modal logic and some of its extensions,  along with an examination of the relationship between these logics and their corresponding relational structures.  These findings are compared to the established results for the classical modal logic.

This research introduces a novel and straightforward system for word-alignment that leverages bilingual data from external sources like machine translation platforms, enabling rapid learning without needing extensive annotated corpora. Our approach can be applied to a wide range of domains and languages, and we demonstrate its effectiveness with translations from Google Translate in English, Spanish, and French. Additionally, we have made our source code freely available on GitHub.

We suggest an distorted resolvent algorithm to solve Nash equilibrium issues, specifically focusing on non-differentiable games with Lipschitz montecarlo potential functions and compact sets, yielding an $\sqrt{k}$ convergence rate, with further applications possible in convex-concave games and quasi-pseudo-monotone games.

I introduce a Python code, PopSyCLE, which calculates the primordial black holes' contribution to dark matter based on a specified mass function and density distribution. This code is adaptable, allowing various mass functions to be incorporated through a base class. Further developments will involve comparing predicted signals from these different functions with observational limits. The code is particularly useful for estimating the production of intermediate-mass primordial black holes, whose creation is potentially induced by the oscillations of a light field, by integrating the corresponding merger rates throughout a density distribution.

We conducted research into the phase behavior of a complex system consisting of wedge-shaped molecules, where each molecule consists of four connected spheres representing the wedge's arms. To investigate the entropic characteristics of this complex system, we applied Monte Carlo methods in various simulation environments. The results revealed a significant phase transition from a hexagonal lattice structure to a modulated spiral pattern, as the wedge's opening angle decreased. Additionally, we discovered two distinct phases with spiral patterns, each characterized by different types of order. Furthermore, the influence of wedge opening on the phase behavior was extensively analyzed.

We've developed novel non-parametric models for large-scale spatial analysis on a global scale, utilizing the Bessel function expansion. These models, called Non-Parametric Bessel Analyses (NBA), operate in a high-dimensional space and are defined by a set of hyperparameters, ensuring the models remain versatile. In this research, we illustrate the effectiveness of NBA by applying it to two prominent spatial problems: forecasting sea surface temperature and modeling Earth's temperature variability. When compared to existing spatial models, NBA demonstrates superior predictive accuracy and improved computational efficiency.

A conventional approach to viewing a quantum state relies heavily on measuring the state itself, which inevitably leads to interpretation difficulties when the state is related to a complex physical phenomenon or an observer-dependent concept. Utilizing undetected photons in a quantum state has the potential to be transformed into a detectable form that can be understood through a simpler, interaction-free process. This process involves using a quantum state and undetected photons to predict the absence of detection in a series of measurements, which can then be linked to a physical reality through a simpler, interaction-free context. Notably, this quantum state and undetected photon relationship can be confirmed using multiple measurement scenarios involving different detection probabilities and a wide range of quantum states and undetected photons pairs. Underscoring the practical applications of this research, it has the potential to address various challenges in quantum information without resorting to complicated interpretation issues related to measurement.

The interaction between a liquid foam and a solid block is studied through a series of experiments that demonstrate how the block's surface gets covered with foam. When the block's surface is smooth, the block's movement causes the foam layer to become compressed and repel the block, resulting in increased friction. In contrast, when the block's surface is rough and covered with fibers, the block's movement leads to the foam layer being stretched and drawn into the space between the block and the surface, resulting in a significant increase in friction that is several times greater than that experienced with smooth surfaces. The key factor contributing to this increased friction appears to be the increased resistance encountered when the foam needs to expand back to its original state, a process that is slowed by the depth of the layer and the size of the openings between the block and the surface. Additionally, the combination of this understanding with a simple mechanical model successfully predicts the stress-strain relationship of this complex system throughout the entire range of deformation.

In medical contexts, outliers or unusual cases often go undetected, leading to incorrect diagnoses. This research proposes a deep learning-based approach to identify atypical skin cancer samples, with the goal of enhancing diagnostic accuracy. By pinpointing outlier cases, doctors can focus on more unusual lesions, rather than relying solely on common examples. After conducting statistical analysis on the datasets, two entropy-based machine learning models were developed to predict outliers based on entropy values for binary and multi-class classifications. For binary classification, a deep neural network with dropout was used, and for multi-classification, a convolutional neural network with a dropout layer was applied. Both models were trained and tested on the public skin cancer dataset from the ISIC Archive, and the results showed significant accuracy rates of 92% for binary classification and 88% for multi-classification. This research is pivotal because detecting outlier cases could facilitate the development of more accurate deep learning models, improving diagnostic precision in medical imaging.

We measured the lifetime of electrons in sodium using spectro-time spectroscopy.
By applying strain and modifying the density of states at the Fermi level,
we observed electron lifetime variations of 30 percent in different directions.
Our results demonstrate that transport properties can be linked to
electronic behavior near the Fermi level in sodium.

Building on a novel theory, microstate nonequilibrium thermodynamics, we've developed an innovative approach to relate instantaneous nonequilibrium properties of a system during a transition to its initial and final thermodynamic states. This method involves calculating the change in system entropy or heat transfer in terms of phase-space averages of relevant observables along the system's Hamiltonian trajectories. We've demonstrated that these entropy or heat values can be expressed as sums of pairwise contributions, each corresponding to a pair of initial and final microstates. We've overcome a theoretical limitation by developing an entropy change expression that doesn't rely on a particular trajectory trajectory being physical or being in equilibrium. Specifically, we've derived an entropy change formula for a free expanding system that involves an electronic wave packet and a finite potential barrier, and compared it to a benchmark value obtained through a detailed entropy calculation that assumes the system reaches a steady nonequilibrium state. As a result, we've determined the impact of the system's initial condition, the strength of the interaction with the barrier, and the magnitude of the expansion on the predicted entropy change, and validated our approach by showing that the predicted change in entropy during a finite expansion is comparable to the change observed in a steady nonequilibrium state when the system is far removed from the barrier.

This passage provides an in-depth examination of graph weights in connection and curvature forms for a symplectic manifold with Poisson structure that has been deformed using $\hbar$. We introduce a novel generating function, known as the Kontsevich sum, which calculates these weight functions. Our study demonstrates that these weight functions exhibit a pattern of expansion in $\hbar$ and relates to a series expansion of the symplectic potential defined by Bernhard Keller and Martin Grard. We show that connection and curvature graph weights are interconnected and present an explicit formula for them by induction.

We explore solitary waves known as "nanoptera," characterized by exponentially small oscillations, in two types of precompressed systems: a diatomic chain and a granular chain formed from a precompressed timber-like material. Our analysis focuses on the weak nonlinearity of these systems, where we map the dynamics to a gradient flow and apply the classical singular perturbation method. Our results reveal that the same approach yields similar formulas for the nanoptera, highlighting their universal nature.

New mechanisms are introduced to amplify the cosmological collider's signal, originating from primordial features instead of a smooth inflationary background. This amplification occurs through two processes: the creation of short-lived particles and the constraint on spatial movements imposed by the black hole information paradox. Data from primordial impulses is then analyzed to determine the masses of these particles, assuming a simplified scalar cosmological collider model. This analysis showcases how the cosmological collider's signal can be used to detect heavy particles, even when their direct production is impossible.

This paper delves into the properties of accordion graphs, a specific class of planar, half-torus graphs. The research focuses on determining their Hamiltonicity, a subject not thoroughly explored in graph theory. The findings reveal that only certain classes of accordion graphs possess Hamiltonian cycles, and a criterion is established for the existence of pairings in these graphs. Furthermore, the study compares the structure of accordion graphs to that of quartic circulants, and it is shown that the two are isomorphic under specific conditions.

We carry out a finite-time scaling analysis of quantum walk search on an infinite lattice, where three possible transition probabilities are allowed at any given step. Our results indicate that the survival probability decay is influenced by a combination of two factors: the specific probability distribution used and the nature of the initial state given. Furthermore, our findings reveal that in the scenario of equal probabilities for all possible transitions, a broad class of initial states exhibits the same rate of survival probability decay and also follows a specific scaling law with respect to time. It's noteworthy that this broad class of initial states constitutes an extensive subset of all possible initial states. Additionally, our analysis shows that in the scenario of equal probabilities for all possible transitions, a broad class of initial states exhibits the same rate of survival probability decay and also follows a specific scaling law with respect to time, which is identical to that observed in the context of the one-state search algorithm. Our results are validated through both analytical and numerical approaches.

Vision transformers are currently receiving significant attention due to their superior performance in various computer vision tasks. In comparison to convolutional neural networks, they have shown impressive results in numerous applications, including image classification, semantic segmentation, and object detection. Although the advantages of vision transformers over convolutional neural networks have been well-documented, the benefits of using self-supervised learning on these models are less clear. In our paper, we investigate the effect of self-supervised learning on vision transformers by introducing the Emerging Features model, which combines the principles of self-supervised learning and multi-layer perception-based feature extractors. The results of our experiments reveal the occurrence of an important phenomenon called "emergence" in the learning process of vision transformers, where complex attributes appear as a result of self-supervised learning. The recognition of these complex attributes surpasses that of supervised learning, while also being robust to random initializations and various transformation parameters. Furthermore, the insights gained from our analysis suggest a positive correlation between the degree of emergence and the model's capacity.

A new cosmological model is presented, which incorporates two types of dark energy to address the unresolved problems within the Lambda-CDM model and a novel unified dark energy hypothesis. This doughnut-shaped hypothesis suggests that dark energy transitions from a "stiff" fluid at low density to a "sticky" fluid at high density. A dynamical system is established to simulate the interaction between these two distinct forms of dark energy. Simulation results indicate that the sticky phase acts as a cosmological sink, absorbing anisotropic pressure and resolving issues within the Lambda-CDM model, such as the underreduction age discrepancy problem. Additionally, this model aligns with the Baryon Acoustic Oscillation feature at the zenith in the deceleration parameter graph.

We present a straightforward proof that in three or more dimensions, the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Euler equations has an inherent issue of instability in certain types of high-frequency initial data, even within the most general framework of Sobolev spaces. Specifically, in the most general framework of Sobolev spaces, we demonstrate that the solution to the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Euler equations is not only highly dependent on the initial data but also cannot be modified to obtain a general solution for all possible initial data, even within the most general framework of Sobolev spaces.

Recent breakthroughs in text-to-image and image-to-image transformations have led to remarkable creations, often producing images that closely match a description but also include unnecessary and distracting elements. Current models fail to produce stable results consistent with a description, highlighting the importance of semantic guidance in the latent space of these models. The stable creator, a semantic editor, is an innovative tool that navigates this space to produce consistent creations from varying inputs like images, texts, and semantic templates. Developed through the combination of two diffusion models, a semantic editor is capable of refining the semantic representation of images and restoring high-quality features of existing images. The editor's effectiveness is demonstrated through creations that precisely incorporate a description and eliminate distractions in real photographs, as well as consistent creations of abstract semantic templates and new image styles. Furthermore, the stable creator offers numerous practical applications across multiple domains, continually producing innovative and consistent creations.

This research introduces an innovative method, known as Reversible Concealment (RC), for data protection by encrypting input data and reversibly encrypting the encryption keys. In this study, a novel approach utilizing Bayesian Neural Networks is proposed to achieve RC with keys that can be safely transmitted over public networks. Furthermore, we investigate the conditions required to maintain data integrity and ensure its retrievability even in the presence of adversarial attacks. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our RC method by protecting various image datasets against diverse types of perturbations.

Our research investigates the implications of the $J/\psi$ particle decaying into invisible matter on light vector bosons and Majorana neutrinos. To understand these phenomena, we analyze the rate at which $J/\psi$ decays into a photon and invisible matter, as well as the ratio of this process to $J/\psi$ decaying into a photon and electron-positron pairs. We found that the present experimental limits on this decay mode permit the mass of a hypothetical vector boson to range from $B$ masses of around $10^{-3}$ eV to $10^{-8}$ eV, which represents a significant expansion over the current LHCb collaboration's findings. Additionally, we found that the observed limits on this decay process allow for the mass of a hypothetical neutrino to range from $B$ masses of around $10^{-3}$ eV to $10^{-9}$ eV, which represents a significant expansion over the current Perlmutter et al. (2006) findings. We also examined the observability of dark matter production in the $J/\psi$ decaying into invisible matter at future experiments, including the BEPCII, the SuperKEKB, the Belle II with its upgraded luminosity, and the future electron-positron collider with high luminosity. We found that these experiments could potentially produce between $10^4$ and $10^9\) dark matter events per inverse barns of luminosity, depending on the mass

The Sun's photosphere and lower atmospheric layers contain tiny magnetic bright points (MBPs) that are thought to be caused by the emergence of new magnetic flux. These areas exhibit extremely high magnetic field strengths and are essential for coronal heating, as they efficiently convert electrical energy into heat. Understanding the basic properties of MBPs is vital for this process, but it is hindered by the lack of accurate involution models. It has been suggested that two-part distributions could effectively describe the properties of these areas, providing a better physical representation. This study uses high-resolution data from the SOT/Hinode and the GREGOR telescope to examine the area, brightness, and distribution patterns of MBPs, with the goal of verifying the previous hypothesis. The results show that both observations describe the area and brightness of these points accurately, highlighting their distinct patterns. Furthermore, two-part distributions are found to be adequate in describing the area and brightness of these points, as well as their overall frequency. This discovery is accompanied by the suggestion that MBPs are composed of separate areas with different physical characteristics, necessitating a more detailed and effective model to accurately represent their properties.

Fast flow patterns can be generated through two methods, either by minimizing the velocity vector's magnitude or by optimizing a distance function while constraining velocity at boundary points. Research previous to this study analyzed human visual processing using the latter approach. This study reverses the paradigm, using the former method to simulate fast flow patterns that resemble those observed in human behavior. The results suggest that both processing methods rely on similar structural characteristics to generate similar patterns of integration. The findings of this study align with previous research on computational models of human visual processing and the statistical properties of minimal films match the data distribution of perceived flow patterns. The outcomes of this study also provide a new method for testing the hypothesis that local maxima in the flow pattern's critical points are necessary for object recognition.

Dark particles interacting through Abelian gauge symmetries can explain the persistence of large-scale magnetic fields in the universe through a breaking cycle that involves magnetic flux freezing. We investigate the possibility that these dark particles are stable and regular, and thus constitute "magical" dark matter. In particular, we examine how the breaking of dark magnetic symmetry by skyrmions affects the mass of these dark particles, and find that heavy dark particles with masses greater than the MeV range are constrained by big-bang nucleosynthesis, whereas those with lower masses are restricted by observations of galaxy rotations and the universe's age. Additionally, we consider the implications of electromagnetic interactions between dark particles and ordinary matter, and find that these interactions do not significantly alter the limits obtained from the aforementioned observations. Lastly, we outline a potential discovery path for these magnetic monopoles using underground detectors sensitive to low-energy nuclear interactions.

The rapidly evolving field of weather forecasting through deep learning has reached a new milestone with the integration of transformer architectures, but they pose a unique challenge to apply to 3D spatiotemporal weather forecasting due to their inherent requirement for sequential input order sensitivity. Traditional transformer models have limited adaptability, necessitating innovative redesigns. Our proposed framework, SWCA, utilizes a distinct windowing strategy on encoded features combined with a dedicated cross-attention mechanism that bypasses order sensitivity issues. By doing so, SWCA enables the direct modeling of spatiotemporal dynamics, significantly outperforming several prominent baseline models in the numerical weather forecasting domain.

In models featuring three Higgs doubles, broken $S_3$ symmetry offers a unique framework for creating stable dark matter particles. However, this setup presents a significant obstacle, as it typically results in dark matter that is too abundant. We demonstrate the feasibility of minimizing such discrepancies by introducing an $S_3$ breaking term, and identify two scenarios that are particularly compelling: one in which the stable dark matter particle has a very low mass, and another where it possesses a negligible interaction with the standard model. Furthermore, we examine the potential for these models to be tested in experiments focusing on lepton flavor non-conservation.

A fundamental assumption in quantum computing known as the PPT quadrilateral conjecture holds that any multi-output computation that produces purely positive results must have at least one input that affects all outputs. Under this assumption, we resolve two longstanding indecisions from Aravind and Branciat's research. Although we're unable to prove the full conjecture, we do demonstrate that any multi-output computation with positive results, coupled with four inputs, can indeed have a input that impacts all outputs. We reach this conclusion by reducing the PPT quadrilateral conjecture to a more manageable hypothesis concerning the behavior of separable operators. Additionally, our research reveals that this new hypothesis is equivalent to the combinatorial PPT conjecture. We also examine the PPT quadrilateral conjecture's relevance to the study of quantum circuits. Notably, the PPT quadrilateral conjecture is deemed particularly vital for understanding the capabilities of quantum circuits equipped with four input outputs.

In complex environments, neurons rely on precise balance between internal transportation needs and capacity to manage excess substances. The optimal equilibrium is achieved through a delicate regulation of molecular transport by modifying transport properties, a process analogous to traffic management. The study of this process involves mathematical modeling, specifically an optimization problem, to analyze how neurons adapt transportation systems in response to changing demands. A key challenge is to identify the most effective modifications, where minimal adjustments yield optimal results, a problem exacerbated by the nonlinear relationship between transport characteristics and the substance distribution issue. To overcome this obstacle, a novel solution approach is proposed, where the optimal solution is linked to the steady-state substance distribution problem through a continuous trajectory of transport parameters, much like in pivot-like movements. The efficiency of this strategy is demonstrated by simulations that highlight its practical value for future research and further investigation into its theoretical underpinnings.

In the realm of finance, networks of assets are frequently analyzed for various purposes, often leading to disparate findings that can make selecting suitable assets a daunting task.  To address this challenge, researchers have created the Net-Work maximizer (NeMo), a algorithmic method for pinpointing assets that exhibit consistent co-occurrence patterns across different network views.  By applying NeMo to the cryptocurrency and stock markets, researchers have discovered notable patterns in assets like Bitcoin, Netflix, and Disney, indicating promising potential for future analysis.  The study validates NeMo's effectiveness through comparative assessments and showcases its capability to streamline asset selection.

In a binary system consisting of a white dwarf and a black hole, a catastrophic event occurs when the white dwarf's outer layers collide with the black hole, causing a massive explosion known as a cataclysmic variable outburst. Our research focuses on the electromagnetic and gravitational waves emitted by the debris clouds during this process, which involves realistic three-dimensional simulations of the interaction between colliding matter. By analyzing the outcome, we find that a significant portion of the material is forcibly drawn into the black hole, resulting in a larger initial outflow compared to earlier estimated values. Approximately 10 percent to 35 percent of the white dwarf's mass is lost in the explosion, and the resulting outflows exhibit densities and velocities consistent with those observed in other compact binary coalescences. Our findings indicate that such events can generate intense electromagnetic radiation in the form of a superluminous supernova, as well as powerful gravitational waves, potentially detectable by advanced gravitational wave detectors. Additionally, the observed emission patterns during these events could be misinterpreted as signs of a neutron star or white dwarf undergoing magnetic polar cap spindown, which would require substantial energy to produce the observed effects.

Three-body $\tau$-decays are examined in this study, focusing on the hadronic component.  The research undertakes a detailed analysis of the $V-A$ structure of the hadronic currents, leading to a formulation of the Form Factors, based on the assumption of this structure.  The formulation includes ten distinct Form Factors, each computed using the Calculus on Finite Fields techniques.  The numerical evaluation of the FF is carried out within the isospin symmetry framework.  Additionally, this work presents QCD corrections to the FF, computed using the Finite Field Regularization method.  The first order corrections include six distinct form factors, with the remaining four corrected by the weak effective pointlike interaction.  The publication concludes with a brief discussion on the application of these findings in $\tau$-decays.

Jim\'enez, Becerra, and Gelbukh (2013) introduced the "symmetric Tversky distance", utilizing a formula that involves parameters $S_{A,B}$, $\alpha$, and $\beta$. However, this formula's selection is unclear, as stated in Theorem 1, which instead proposes an alternative expression for $S_{A,B}$. Consequently, a family of parametrized metrics is defined by theorems 2 and 3. Specifically, setting $\alpha = \beta$ yields the "weighted Tversky distance", previously studied in Alcalde and Raghavan (2013) and proven to be a metric space in Raghavan (2016). In contrast, our approach sets $\alpha = 1 - \beta$, which, combined with previous results, implies that $S_{A,B}$ is both a metric and satisfying the triangle inequality when $B \cap S(A \cup B) \neq \emptyset$. Furthermore, theorems 4 and 5 demonstrate that $S_{A,B}$ is both a metric and satisfying the triangle inequality in certain probabilistic spaces, even in the absence of $B \cap S(A \cup B)$. Ultimately, theorems 6 and 7 show that $S_{A,B}$ is both a metric and satisfying the triangle inequality when $A \subset B$.

Modern motion de-blurring methods based on deep learning utilize real-world data to train a model, either by applying the model directly to an deblurred dataset or by incorporating an auxiliary task to counteract over-smoothing effects.  In this paper, we introduce an innovative approach to motion de-blurring that doesn't rely on real-world data. Instead, an auxiliary model is trained to mimic the effects of actual blur processes, allowing it to reverse even extreme cases of blurring with minimal supervision. Furthermore, our method naturally resists over-smoothing. We have conducted extensive testing on a variety of natural and artificial scenes and the results demonstrate that our method is highly effective even when the blurring is extremely severe.

We explore the possibility of mimicking a leaky integrate-and-fire neuron, the fundamental building block of many biological neural networks, through the synthesis of multiple chemical reaction systems. These systems, modeled after widely accepted reaction mechanisms for DNA-based catalyzed self-reproduction, are designed to replicate a specific pattern of DNA molecules over time periods comparable to those of biological neurons. We then apply these reaction systems to simulate either random spike patterns or specific neuron responses to changing light intensity, utilizing multiple copies of the reaction system to simulate different membrane conductances and ion channel behaviors.

The ultrapower of any ordered set is created by taking the family of ultrapowers from its elements, and this process results in an extremely intricate and complex structure with numerous intricate properties.  When examining the continuity within the ultrapower of any ordered set, it becomes apparent that the concept of continuity is defined by a system of inductive axioms, and understanding these inductions enables us to grasp the nature of the ultrapower.  By inducing the definition of continuity in a novel way, we are able to uncover a fundamental theorem regarding the continuity of the ultrapower of any ordered set.  Furthermore, our findings also pertain to the total order in the ultrapower of any ordered set, and we demonstrate that the total order is continuous if and only if the original ordered set is continuous.  By incorporating an additional ingredient, namely the chain index, we are able to generalize our previous conclusions, and this new perspective allows us to understand the nature of the total order in the ultrapower of any ordered set, and we are able to establish a precise limit for the total order in the ultrapower of any ordered set when taking into account chains.

Scientific breakthroughs in data-driven science increasingly rely on applying sophisticated AI models to comprehensive, discipline-specific datasets. However, the general profiling of these datasets raises important implications for fair machine learning, as it can lead to the exclusion of certain data subjects from beneficial models. Given the absence of standardized guidelines for profiling in science, we suggest that each research community should establish its own guidelines for dataset profiling, taking into account the unique characteristics of their datasets and the potential consequences for their stakeholders. By promoting more targeted and responsible profiling, we can foster more inclusive and equitable machine learning models in science.

Hadwiger's Coloring Conjecture asserts that every graph with t colors includes a complete graph with t vertices. This has been reinforced by another theory suggesting if a graph is defined by t colored triangles, then a complete graph with t vertices must exist within it. A previous study demonstrated the reevaluation of this theory and proved its validity for graphs with 4 and 5 colored triangles. This new finding supports Hadwiger's original assumption and provides a new mathematical concept.

This research introduces an advanced algorithm for smoothly reconstructing graph signal data based on the generalized correntropy criterion, with the added benefit of adaptive kernel width adjustment. The GGS-KW algorithm utilizes the generalized correntropy with a kernel width that changes dynamically, thereby effectively reducing noise and improving signal reconstruction. In particular, the kernel width is set apart and optimized using the kernel alignment criterion, with its value determined through a data-driven approach. By adjusting the kernel width in this way, the GGS-KW algorithm achieves improved performance compared to traditional smoothing methods. Moreover, the computational complexity of the GGS-KW algorithm is analyzed, and it is demonstrated via exhaustive experiments that this algorithm outperforms existing graph signal reconstruction methods across diverse scenarios and environments.

Theoretical research suggests creating long-lived entangled spinor atoms to enhance the sensitivity of magnetic field measurements in atomic interferometry. In practical applications, generating these entangled states is often challenging due to noise from various sources, and experiments struggle to achieve the optimal results predicted by theory. Our experiment using a specially designed method for entanglement generation has achieved significant improvements in magnetic field measurement sensitivity, and has yielded results comparable to those predicted by theory, showcasing an over 43 times improvement in sensitivity. This enhancement is attributed to minimizing random noise during the entanglement generation process.

The focus of this research is on the first eigenvalue of the first eigenvalue problem for the nonlinear Robin boundary value problem in the given space. By utilizing techniques from optimal transportation, including the Caffarelli-Sobolev inequality, we derive precise upper and lower bounds for this eigenvalue in terms of the given data. Our approach also enables us to derive comparable estimates for the first eigenvalue of the Dirichlet problem under assumptions on the nonlinear function that involve $\Delta_2$-condition and monotonicity.

Deep Neural Networks have eclipsed traditional signal processing methods like classical matched filtering, yet the success of Graph Convolutional Neural Networks is less understood. We compare GCNNs to a simple matched filtering approach, revealing that GCNNs with full connectivity and no bias can be interpreted as applying a matched filter on a weighted sum of the input nodes. The weighted sum aggregates node features based on degree centrality, treating all nodes as equivalent and using the same importance. In contrast, the biased GCNN incorporates additional variables, effectively acting as a directed filtering method. We illustrate the limitations of biased GCNNs through flawed predictions and inadequate representation of ground truth. These insights may guide the development of improved graph-based deep learning models.

A novel approach called deep contextualized self-learning for dependency parsing is introduced, specifically designed for low-resource languages. The method incorporates self-training, leveraging tag and dependency annotation patterns from related languages to fill parsing gaps in new languages. A key element is the introduction of a dependency annotation encoder, a part of the model's parameter set, which enhances the model's ability to learn from annotations in related languages. The proposed system has successfully applied this method to improve dependency parsing in three low-resource languages, achieving notable results that outperform existing benchmarks and showcase the efficacy of this approach for parsing in unfamiliar languages.

We have calculated the semiconductor form factors for $B\to D\ell\nu_\ell$ using the light-front quark model, with a consistent approach that respects charge confinement. The calculated mass of the $B$ meson is $5277.1$ MeV, close to the experimental value of $5279.2$ MeV. The obtained transition form factors satisfy the constraints of heavy quark effective theory and match the experimental outcomes for $B\to D l\nu_l$ (with $l = e, \mu, \tau$) within the respective uncertainties. The results were also compared to other theoretical predictions, showing a favorable outcome for the Drell-Yan frame, with excellent agreement for most of the form factors; however, some deviation was observed in the spectroscopic frame, particularly for $\mathcal{F}(1)$ and $\mathcal{F}'(2)$. The findings support the use of the light-front quark model as a reliable tool for describing hadronic matrix elements.

We're exploring a theoretical framework known as the applied quantum BRST complex, which provides a robust method for identifying equivalence transformations. Within this context, we identify a specific type of symmetry that arises from the non-reversible nature of certain BRST charges. It's noteworthy that these symmetries are inherently local in character. By examining the local BRST charges, we create a hierarchy of associated symmetries, each with increasing levels of complexity. Our analysis delves into the physical implications of these symmetries and demonstrates their applicability to both flat and curved spacetimes through examples. Additionally, we discuss the relationship between these local BRST charges and the branes that comprise the boundary of the cohomology surface.

Currently, the highest known containment of VNP in NP is related to a property called "non-deterministic polynomial equivalence property with function values". In a recent study, the authors demonstrated that a specific class of problems, which involve comparing the output of two circuits given certain input and context, can be solved through a specific type of logic and is related to VNP. Additionally, the study offered a more detailed examination of a specific class of problems, which involve determining the equivalence or differences between two circuits, and established their relationship to a class of problems solvable through a specific type of logic. Furthermore, the study presented a more detailed examination of a class of problems, which involve determining the equivalence or differences between two circuits of the same size or two circuits of varying sizes, and established their relationship to a class of problems solvable through a specific type of logic. In the context of two circuits of the same size, the study also found a connection to a class of problems solvable through a specific type of logic that only considers certain aspects of the circuit structure. In a broader sense, the study also found connections between these problem classes and the properties of directed graph classes. Specifically, the study found that the properties of certain digraph classes and the properties of the above-mentioned circuit classes exhibit a striking similarity. In particular, the study established a comprehensive classification system for digraphs based on their properties and simultaneously provided a comprehensive classification system for the above-mentioned circuit classes based on their properties.

In a compound known as pyrochlore iridates, specifically (Eu1-xBix)2Ir2O7, a transition from an insulating state to a metallic state is observed as the amount of bismuth increases. This transformation is attributed to the alteration of spin-orbit coupled 5d orbitals in iridium, which results in a highly correlated system. Utilizing high-resolution core-level spectra from a focused x-ray beam, our study reveals the effects of correlated behavior and Mott-Hubbard physics on this insulating-to-metal transition. Specifically, we analyze the changes to core-level spectra using a model that accounts for final-state interactions, which provides insight into the behavior of correlated 5d electrons in pyrochlore iridates.

Consider a metric space ${\mathfr M}$ equipped with a metric $d$, a natural numbers $n\geq 1$, and a finite dimensional vector space ${\mathbb R}^k$ with a norm $|\cdot|$. For the mapping $f$, define its $\varepsilon$-selection as ${\rm Sel}_\varepsilon(f)$, which consists of all Lipschitz mappings $s:{\mathfr M}\to{\mathbb R}^k$ satisfying the condition $\mbox{dist}(s(x),f(x))\leq\varepsilon$ for all $x\in{\mathfr M}$. When ${\mathfr M}$ is a topological space, we study closed bounded subsets of the mapping's $\varepsilon$-selection, and specifically, the properties of its core ${\rm Co}_\varepsilon(f)$, which consists of all $x\in{\mathfr M}$ for which there is a neighborhood $U$ satisfying $\mbox{dist}(s(x),f(x))\leq\varepsilon$ for all $s\in{\rm Sel}_\varepsilon(f)$ and $s(x)\in s({\mathfr M})$. We establish the sufficient and necessary conditions for the existence of the core, and then this result is applied to analyze the properties of Lipschitz selections of set-valued mappings defined from the Hilbert space

The purpose of this paper is to explore the possibilities of constructing likelihood functions that exhibit cyclic and non-transitive properties. We first establish a fundamental condition for likelihood functions, and then design a sample space and measurement tool to facilitate the creation of such likelihood functions. Through a straightforward example, we demonstrate the existence of a non-transitive likelihood that is proportional to the geometric distribution. Furthermore, we provide an example of a cyclic likelihood that is based on a discrete distribution with a memory component of two.

In the realm of meta-programming, a compile-time component can scrutinize a program's compile-time structure. Our experimental research delves into an innovative approach where a compile-time element proactively identifies and eliminates unnecessary aspects of a program's runtime configuration at compile time. Our findings indicate that a substantial portion - approximately 75% - of the runtime parameters in widely-used benchmark programs remain unaltered and can be eliminated prior to deployment. Utilizing our newly-developed framework, which integrates meta-programming and reachability analysis, we meticulously identify and erase these superfluous runtime settings from the program's code. Through extensive benchmarking, we formally verify that the modified programs 1) operate within predetermined bounds, 2) exhibit no runtime stack overflow, and 3) accurately reflect the original program execution, thus rendering the unnecessary runtime parameters redundant. Consequently, this reduction in runtime complexity translates to a notable enhancement in runtime efficiency - a remarkable improvement of up to 2.16 times faster execution speed in certain cases, and consistently surpasses alternative minimalization techniques by as much as 1.25 times faster execution speed.

Light dark matter particles are capable of interacting with nuclei through the exchange of a scalar mediator, and this interaction can be studied experimentally by analyzing the recoil energies of nuclei. However, high recoil energies result in fewer event occurrences, limiting the sensitivity of such experiments to a particular range of mass and interaction strength. We present a new approach to this problem in our paper, proposing that instead of focusing solely on nuclear recoils, the same interaction can be explored by looking at the kinetic energy of electrons released during nuclear scattering. By doing so, we can significantly increase the sensitivity of direct detection experiments to a particular range of mass and interaction strength. We provide numerical results illustrating how this new approach could impact existing and future experiments, and show that it could potentially allow for the detection of sub-GeV dark matter particles.

This paper examines the dynamics of a two-level atom interacting with a cavity mode in the presence of amplitude damping, utilizing the non-Hermitian Hamiltonian developed by Sudarshan. We derived analytical solutions for the time-evolved state of the system and calculated key quantum mechanical properties such as entanglement, transmission capacity, and Rabi oscillations in both initial and thermal states. Our findings indicate that entanglement decay is accompanied by Rabi oscillations and that an initial number of photons greater than one prevents Rabi oscillations in the atom's probability amplitude. Additionally, transmission and Rabi oscillations can be restored in both the atom and the cavity mode by adjusting the Rabi constant.

Measuring inter-beat intervals from ECG signals can provide early warnings for cardiovascular diseases. However, identifying IBIs from noisy signals is difficult, especially when they are heavily distorted by motion noise, which is common in individuals who are highly active. Researchers working on remote health monitoring and wearable devices have identified signal denoising and IBI estimation as a significant area of focus. Recent breakthroughs have involved the use of deep learning, which has significantly improved signal quality and subsequent IBI accuracy, outperforming former approaches that relied on traditional statistical methods. A novel deep learning architecture known as Tiramisu has shown great promise in tackling difficult machine learning challenges, and in this research, it is successfully applied to the difficult task of estimating IBIs from heavily distorted signals. Our experimental protocol tested four different denoising techniques that combine deep learning with classical approaches and achieved remarkable results, with the Tiramisu-based approach achieving nearly perfect accuracy and significantly outperforming competing deep learning models.

We examine the Active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck particle model, which is a theoretical model used to analyze the complex movements of active particles. Our analysis focuses on the temporal fluctuations of the work performed by a force exerted on such a particle, active or passive, over the course of its motion. We derive both general, theoretical fluctuations and specific numerical fluctuations for this work using numerical simulations. These results demonstrate the existence of two distinct regimes in which the fluctuations of the work performed vary significantly. When the particle is softly actuated, the fluctuations of the work converge with thermal fluctuations of an equilibrium system, regardless of the particle type. Conversely, when the particle is strongly actuated, the fluctuations of the work are significantly higher than those of a thermal equilibrium system and are characterized by a specific power law and depend on multiple factors, including the particle type, the force applied, and the time elapsed. Additionally, our numerical simulations reveal that the fluctuations of the work performed by a soft actuation are bounded by a specific equation and depend on the force, the particle type, and the time elapsed. These findings indicate that both the work performed by a soft actuation and the corresponding thermal equilibrium fluctuations can be described by a specific equation, known as a universal law, and that these fluctuations are characterized by a specific time-variation pattern, known as a time variant.

This research introduces HUMBI, a large-scale, comprehensive multiview dataset consisting of gestures performed by eight individuals captured using 20 sophisticated cameras arranged in a horseshoe configuration. Unlike existing datasets that typically record a limited number of views, HUMBI features a diverse collection of high-quality, 3D human body performances from multiple viewpoints. Our primary goal in creating HUMBI is to enhance the understanding of human movement through computer vision and provide a valuable resource for developing computer vision-based human movement analysis and generation capabilities. In support of HUMBI, we have established the HUMBI Challenge, a benchmark competition focused on leveraging deep multiview gesture recognition models to achieve top performance. The HUMBI Challenge offers three distinct tracks, each centered on generating specific computer vision-based skills, such as predicting 3D human body keypoints, performingning gesture recognition, and producing 3D human body performances. The HUMBI dataset and challenge are now available online at the specified URLs: https://umbi.org.

The surge in cross-lingual model transfer has led to the consensus that contextual representation models are more effective than phrase-based models. Nonetheless, transferring such models from high-resource languages to low-resource languages remains a daunting task. Moreover, accurately identifying a word's target language remains a persistent challenge. In response to these issues, this paper presents a novel approach that utilizes neural task representations as weak guidance for facilitating model-agnostic cross-lingual transfer. By incorporating neural task representations into the training process, this paper achieves state-of-the-art results on XLT benchmarks, including 92.67% XQT-5 and 95.25% GLUE-multilingual ensemble benchmarks. Notably, the proposed method has been successfully applied to both E2E-Dialog and NLP tasks, demonstrating its versatility and effectiveness.

A common approach in video super-resolution is the recurrent structure, with the BasicVSR method being one of the top-performing frameworks, leveraging careful frame selection and alignment to achieve high-quality results for low-FPS video enhancement. In an enhanced version called BasicVSR++, researchers refine these techniques by simplifying frame selection, implementing a more efficient propagation method, and optimizing alignment, ultimately resulting in faster processing times with comparable results to state-of-the-art models. The improved framework achieves this through accurate motion estimation using the VINSF model and reduced memory requirements, achieving a significant speed increase of 3.7 times while preserving high accuracy. The source code for BasicVSR++ is available on the GitHub repository at https://github.com/NovelCorporation/BasicVSR/.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using a
single-trained dynamics model leads to significant performance losses when learning
multiple tasks at the same time. Through closer analysis, we identify the root
cause as catastrophic interference - the degradation of task capabilities by
means of overwriting previous knowledge. To overcome this, we propose modular
networks as a solution, allowing a substantial improvement in learning multiple
tasks using a single model.

We have reexamined the performance of heat engines operating within specific timeframes, taking into consideration varying levels of heat exchange and mechanical work production. Utilizing a universal method for calculating efficiency based on heat distribution, we found that the maximum work achieved over a fixed time can be maximized by allowing one heat source's temperature to fluctuate within specific limits, provided the other heat source's temperature remains constant. This optimization outcome aligns with experimental and theoretical research indicating the most effective strategy involves thermal regulation. To validate our theoretical model, we conducted two sets of experiments, one employing a laboratory-based setup and the other a computational simulation, which both validated the theoretical predictions.

This research proposes a spatial analysis for assessing the impact of hurricanes and storm surges on power systems. To simulate the temporal and spatial progression of hurricanes and storm surges, a combined approach using real-world weather models and mathematical formulas is utilized. By integrating geographical information, specific hurricane scenarios can be modeled to determine areas affected by storm surges, up to 300 kilometers inland, and factors such as wind speed and direction. These conditions are applied to electrical power systems, similar to traditional reliability assessments, but with adjustments to account for spatially distributed weather patterns. To illustrate the effectiveness of this method, a 2000-bus test system is utilized and analyzed under different hurricane scenarios.

This research proves a variant of the Three Balls Theorem for functions $f$ and $g$, which are harmonic duals in Euclidean space, using a complex structure. The proof leverages a recent independent verification of the original Three Balls Conjecture for eigenfunctions in Clifford analysis by V. Souplet and L. Boudin.

We examine a class of parameter-dependent area-preserving maps, derived from baker transformations with alternating modes of scaling and translation, and investigate the evolution of maximal entropy measures as these parameters vary. These maps can be likened to random walks on binary trees, analogous to a system previously studied by Durr and Stein, which yields two distinct dynamical scenarios: one in which entropy remains accessible and another in which it precipitates a catastrophic decline. In the context of the Dyck system, this transition marks a shift from ergodicity to periodic behavior. Crucially, the endpoints of this entropy degradation route coincide with two separate fixed points for the mapping, one of which exhibits a peculiar stochastic appearance despite being deterministic in origin.

Following the discovery of the Higgs boson in 2012, the next step in particle physics is to delve deeper into the Standard Model and its expanded scalar sectors. This review covers various methods used to investigate expanded scalar sectors, including global fits and individual searches, focusing on the roles of future collider experiments and astrophysical observations in this quest.

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet), an improved version of WaveNet, to enhance speech synthesis performance in terms of naturalness and efficiency. The key enhancements include a pitch-dependent filter bank, a refined activation function, and a data-driven quantization table. The outcome is a more realistic speech output, particularly in terms of its spectral and temporal characteristics. The effectiveness of this model was confirmed through objective and subjective evaluations using a vast Chinese speech corpus.

Recommender Systems face a persistent issue of providing accurate recommendations that cater to each user's unique preferences, while accounting for the inherent subjectivity involved. Given the inherent complexities, recommenders struggle to effectively leverage both content and user characteristics. In an attempt to address these challenges, this paper proposes an innovative bicluster-based recommendation approach, tailored to the needs of data sparse and preference diverse environments. By employing an unsupervised biclustering method, our approach identifies and leverages user-specific biclusters, characterized by distinct preferences across multiple content attributes. These biclusters are then utilized to develop personalized recommendation lists for each user, comprised of content items clustered together by their inherent characteristics and corresponding to the user's preferred preferences. The efficacy of our approach is demonstrated through exhaustive experiments on two real-world datasets, where it surpasses the performance of relevant state-of-the-art recommendation systems, and showcases its robustness through thorough hyper-parameter analysis and qualitative evaluations.

Gershman and Killip conducted new research on solar magnetic activity, incorporating high-resolution spectra from the HARPS-N solar telescope between 2010 and 2014. By analyzing various indicators related to magnetic activity on the sun, they investigated their connections and tested potential correlations with frequency patterns in the spectra. The results revealed significant connections between indicators and frequency patterns, allowing for the identification of active and quiet solar periods in the data. The study demonstrated that combining these indicators can improve the understanding and prediction of solar magnetic activity.

To differentiate between zero-energy peaks originating from Majorana and those from other causes at non-zero temperatures, our approach focuses on resistive tunneling spectroscopy with heat dissipation. Our analysis shows that Majorana's distinctive parity-dependent tunneling behavior remains intact even when coupled with Ohmic dissipation. By measuring the average number of phonons during tunneling and incorporating the scanning electron microscope's intrinsic resistance, we can accurately detect the Majorana peak across various dissipation strengths and temperatures. Our study demonstrates that Ohmic dissipation does not obscure the parity-dependent signature characteristic of Majorana islands.

The theory of topological Markov processes serves as a dynamic equivalent to the study of hyperbolic surface maps, with geometric insights gaining an enhanced understanding through its topological framework. Recent breakthroughs by Brisebarre-Chaillou-Gérard and Danino-Ben-Arous-Douziech-Gérd have identified specific bicategorical characteristics for these processes, with the latter research additionally discovering new invariant phenomena of limited computational nature. Building upon Brisebarre-Corbani's previous findings, this current work establishes that the pointed bicategorical Markov sheets of these processes effectively encode the hyperbolic characteristics present on their trace maps, further revealing how these bicategorical invariants can be utilized to analyze the emerging patterns of hyperbolic characteristics during the decomposition of surface maps into their associated Markov processes.

Current approaches to colorize black and white images are hindered by the absence of a universal solution, necessitating the selection of specific colorization techniques for each picture. Although certain methods excel at restoring historical images, others may produce unappealing results on modern photographs. A key factor contributing to these disparate outcomes is the distinct style inherent in each image, which if identified and extracted, could enable the development of a style-preserving image colorizer. In this research, a novel neural network architecture called SPCN is proposed, designed to extract the style from a pair of images. By distilling the style in this way, a specific and adaptable solution can be created for a wide range of colorization tasks. Additionally, the paper introduces a new benchmark called LHS, which assesses a colorizer's performance based on its overall consistency. Based on these new metrics and models, a comprehensive comparison of various colorization techniques is presented, along with the creation of style-specific colorizers, all of which can be accessed at the provided website.

This technical report showcases the winning model of the AQTC task, recently introduced in the LOVEU challenge at CVPR 2022, where the team achieved high-ranking placements across multiple evaluation metrics. 

The proposed model leverages a novel multi-head attention-based architecture, incorporating an auxiliary loss to effectively address data shortages during training. Notably, the winning model's primary feature differentiates it from alternative methods is its utilization of attention mechanisms in both encoder and decoder components. 

To facilitate reproducibility, the report includes detailed information on both the contest's dataset characteristics and the proposed model's training procedures. Moreover, the report discusses the effectiveness of various techniques implemented to enhance the model's performance, particularly the integration of auxiliary loss and utilizing attention mechanisms. 

The results obtained from both quantitative evaluation and qualitative analysis demonstrate the superiority of the proposed model when compared to alternative methods, showcasing its high quality through extensive experimental validation.

The intricate process of snowfall is heavily influenced by atmospheric turbulence, which causes snow particles to deviate from their straight fall paths. As a result, particles interact with one another mid-air, leading to altered trajectories that depend on their sizes. Through high-resolution simulations using a new mathematical model, researchers have recreated atmospheric turbulence and studied its effects on small snow particles. By analyzing these particles' behaviors, scientists discovered changes in their vertical speed patterns, indicating faster falling speeds for larger particles, despite all particles starting with the same initial downward velocity. These findings demonstrate the presence of selective sweeping, a phenomenon in which larger particles move downward more quickly than smaller ones, potentially explaining earlier observations of particle size variations in snowfields.

As robots move around their environment, they gather initial information which they then use for planning their course. Existing solutions involve two main approaches: either the trajectory is determined first and then executed, or the path is continuously adjusted on the go. While the former method uses more accurate navigation but is slower, the latter is faster but has worse navigation accuracy. In light of this, we suggest an approach that is both accurate and efficient by leveraging deep neural networks. After an initial prediction of the trajectory, the route is modified in real-time based on the actual progress towards the destination. This process involves re-predicting the future path based on the current position and previous trajectories, which are fed into the model. By focusing on this constant adjustment, the complexity of the navigation task is simplified and the results show significant reductions in computation time while maintaining high levels of accuracy. This concept has been successfully applied and tested in simulation and with real-world data collected by a mobile robot.

In industrial applications like defect detection, researchers are finding that three-dimensional sparse time-projection convolution (3D SPTC) is an ideal neural network architecture for analyzing complex point-cloud data. Despite its effectiveness, this model poses significant computational challenges and data transmission costs. Our study focuses on addressing these inefficiencies through an innovative approach that leverages bicephalous convolutional autoencoders (BCAEs). By employing a BCAE-based autoencoder, we can substantially diminish the size of the training data, thereby reducing computational requirements and data transmission costs for 3D SPTC networks. Our novel data reduction framework consists of two key components: an encoder that converts an image into a reduced-dimensional binary code, and a decoder that reconstructs the original image using this code. To prevent code dequantization distortion and ensure accurate decoder reconstruction, we utilize supplementary head networks. Our results demonstrate that the proposed BCAE-based autoencoder yields high-quality reconstructions of binary codes and enables efficient data reduction for 3D SPTC networks.

The Finzi model, built upon gravity's hierarchical nature, poses an interesting alternative to conventional self-similar models. By incorporating non-hierarchical components, it offers a more realistic glimpse into the formation and structure of galaxy clusters. By mapping the external gravitational potential to electronic signals, researchers can compare simulated data to actual X-ray observations of these structures. On a larger scale, this modeling technique facilitates a systematic examination of gravitational effects, bridging the gap between fundamental science and applied physics. In this study, a colloquation with the Navarro, Frenk and White model, it presents a more detailed analysis of galaxy clusters' internal distribution and density, setting the stage for further research into their thermal states.
